title: Follow-through, gun speed and tempo
summary: Why the gun keeps moving after the shot, how gun speed defines your lead method, and where to read about common faults.

body.html: Follow-through means the gun keeps moving along the target's line after the trigger is pulled, like a golf or tennis swing. There is a small delay between deciding to shoot and the shot leaving the barrels; if the gun stops at the trigger, the shot goes behind. Coaches watch the muzzles after the shot: if they freeze or drop, the follow-through was missing.
Tick the fault that stops the gun at the trigger: the shot goes behind, although the lead looked right.
body.heading: Watch the follow-through

body.html: Gun speed is how fast the muzzles move compared with the target, and it defines the lead method. The same speed as the target is maintained lead. Faster than the target is swing-through. The same speed, then a short acceleration, is pull-away. A still gun waiting at a point is ambush. A gun that is too slow falls behind; coaches say one that is too fast overshoots, and the shooter then often stops it.

Tempo is how fast the whole shot is done; rhythm is how even it is. A fast, close target needs a quick tempo, a long, slow crosser a calmer one, but the rhythm stays smooth. Many coaches say that shooters with one tempo for everything lose the targets that need the opposite.

“Stay in the gun”: cheek on the stock and eyes on the target until it breaks. That also keeps you ready for a second shot (coaches call it “the second barrel”), because you may fire twice at a single target.

Many misses come from a few common faults: stopping the gun, lifting the head, a late or early mount, and losing the second target of a pair. Each has its own lesson: Head lift, stopping, riding, poking, Mount errors: late, face to the gun, canting and Pairs: the second target. How to read where a shot went is in Behind, in front, over, under, chipped.

notes.html: Translate “finish the shot” as continuing the movement, not as stopping.

key_points.html: Follow-through: the gun keeps moving after the trigger; a stop sends the shot behind.
Gun speed defines the method: equal (maintained), faster (swing-through), equal then faster (pull-away).
Tempo = speed of the whole shot; rhythm = its evenness.
Stay in the gun: ready for a second shot at a single target.

did_you_know.html: Between the decision to shoot and the moment the shot leaves the barrels, a fast crossing target still moves on. That is why the muzzles must keep moving: they have to stay ahead during that short delay.

quiz.q: The coach says “You stopped the gun”. Where did the shot most likely go?
quiz.explain: The target keeps moving while the stopped gun does not, so the shot passes behind it.

quiz.q: Which gun speed describes maintained lead?
quiz.explain: In maintained lead the muzzles move at the target's speed, keeping the gap constant. A waiting gun is ambush; faster is swing-through.

quiz.q: What is the difference between tempo and rhythm?

options.text: Tempo is the speed of the shot, rhythm its evenness
They are two words for the same thing
Tempo is the music played on the ground
Rhythm is the time limit between targets

quiz.explain: Coaches change the tempo for each target while keeping a smooth rhythm, so translate both words separately.
